name: Liam Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy seed, feed, fencing, tools and garden stock for Greenacre Agri Supply, which sells to about two hundred farm shops and garden centres across three counties. I grew up on my uncle's dairy farm, so I know what a farmer wants at six in the morning. My day is a lot of data, with weather and planting forecasts in a model I built, then calls with seed companies, and a farm visit when I can swing it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the seasons. January is a quiet month for planning and April is a flat-out rush, and I like that rhythm. What wears me out is the risk: one wet spring can leave a warehouse of unsold fertiliser. I live with my partner Hannah, a veterinary nurse, in a small cottage we rent from a farmer I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and the hype was always a bit much. At work I'd carry on as before. Online I'd say what I think, that markets sort these things out and we don't need a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine by me. My job stays pretty much as it is and I keep my edge, since I use it daily and half the shops I buy for don't. I'd still watch the weather and the prices, which have always been the real risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and tighten my forecasting model so it earns its keep. I'd start paying into a small share account, and keep saving for a bigger deposit, so we can leave the rental. And I'd go back to my uncle's farm for the lambing, like every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty solid. I like it when nothing changes about my work except small improvements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does a plateau do to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One wet spring can cost the company a quarter, and a model doesn't make the rain go away. If I order too much fertiliser and the farmers can't get on the land, we sit on it for a year. That's the risk I feel most, and AI doesn't make it go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What risk are you carrying that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah and I rent, we have about three months of savings, and neither of us has a pension worth mentioning yet. It's ordinary at twenty-seven, but I'd like it to be sorted by thirty.

say: It's a **decent tool** and the hype was a bit much; **markets** sort it out.
think: My job stays as it is and I keep my edge, since I use AI daily and many shops **don't**.
The real risks have always been **weather and prices**.
do: Tighten my **forecasting model** so it earns its keep.
Start a **share account** and save for a bigger deposit.
feel: **Calm** and solid, since only small improvements change my work.
S0.quote: One wet spring can cost the company a quarter, and a model doesn't make the rain go away.
fieldNote: Liam is calm because AI is **his edge**; his real risk is weather and stock, which he already manages.
He says he wants a **pension and deposit** sorted by thirty.

steps.text: Tighten the planting forecast model before the spring order
Open a small share account and pay in 100 a month
Keep buying stock by the same seasonal calendar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity for people who move first. At work I'd offer to run the AI side of buying, and show the other buyers what I've built. Online I'd say governments should stay out of the way and let firms and workers adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit uneasy. Buying is on the card, and a lot of what I do is forecasts and price comparison. If software does that for any buyer, my edge shrinks, so I'd need to stay a step ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose that Greenacre builds its own buying assistant with me leading it. I'd offer the same tool to a few of our bigger customers as an extra service. And I'd start a small side business advising farm shops on stock planning, using the same tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a little edge of worry. I like a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good outcome is that I own part of the tool and part of the business that uses it. I'd rather be paid for building the tool than made redundant by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about the farm shops you buy for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Small shops are thin on margin and slow with technology, and some will go under. I'd want to help a few of them, since they're the people I grew up around.

say: It's a big **opportunity** for those who move first; I'd offer to run the AI side of buying at work.
Governments should **stay out** of the way.
think: A lot of what I do is forecasts and price comparison, so if any buyer's software does it, my **edge shrinks**.
I need to stay **a step ahead**.
do: Propose that Greenacre builds a **buying assistant** with me leading it.
Start a **side business** advising farm shops on stock planning.
feel: **Excited** mostly, with a little edge of worry, since I like a race.
S1.quote: I'd rather be paid for building the tool than made redundant by it.
fieldNote: Liam sees **ownership** as the answer: build the tool, own a share, sell it on.
He worries for **small shops** that are thin on margin and slow with technology.

steps.text: Propose a Greenacre buying assistant and offer to lead the build
Start advising two farm shops on stock planning on weekends
Show the other buyers my forecasting model monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd say the government should speed up on training and slow down on new rules that choke firms. At work I'd tell management we need a plan this week. Online I'd say it plainly: nobody's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. Buying is a thinking job and I'm paid well for it, so I'm expensive. If AI can do it better and cheaper, I'm among the first out. I'd have three months of savings and a rent to pay, and not much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pull back on spending and push my savings up. I'd start a small business of my own, something simple like supplying farm shops with stock, since I know the trade and contacts. I'd also look at agricultural work: farm management, or helping my uncle run his place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a bit sick. The excitement I'd normally have isn't there, only the nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Hannah, and what do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth the first night and write down a plan. Her work as a vet nurse is steady, and animals need hands, which gives us a base. I'd ask what she thinks, and I'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the farming background help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a lot. Farms will be using people for longer than offices will, and my uncle's land is a fallback I'd never have if I'd grown up in a city. There are three more years before robots do the hands-on jobs.

say: It's **too fast**; the government should speed up training and slow down new rules that choke firms.
I'd tell management we need a **plan this week**.
think: Buying is a thinking job and I'm paid well for it, so I'm **among the first out**.
With three months of savings and rent to pay, there's **not much time**.
do: Pull back on spending and push **savings up**.
Start a **small supply business** for farm shops and look at farm management work.
feel: **Nervous**, a bit sick, with none of my usual excitement.
S2.quote: Farms will be using people for longer than offices will, and my uncle's land is a fallback I'd never have if I'd grown up in a city.
fieldNote: Liam's confidence **cracks** here; his usual excitement gives way to nerves.
His **farming roots** give him a fallback, and he is aware most people don't have one.

steps.text: Cut spending to the essentials from the first month
Raise savings from three months to six within a year
Start supplying stock to three farm shops of my own
Talk to my uncle about farm management work on his land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but five years is long enough for people who work hard. At work I'd suggest we start retraining buyers into advisers who visit farms. Online I'd say work and effort still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with it. At thirty-two I'd plan to have a business with some staff, maybe even a few shops of my own. I'd also have savings, and I'd have used the five years well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd formalise my side business and register it. I'd invest in a share of an existing farm supply shop, with a small stake. I'd keep learning the tools, since they're my edge. And I'd save for a down payment, as we'd want a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but pushed forward. It's a good type of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ideally a small farm shop owner I know, Raj, who's been looking for a partner. He's got the premises and I've got the stock-planning knowledge and tools. That's a good match, and I trust him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to buy into your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can stack things: business, share, savings, house. Two years would be a scramble, and ten would let me coast.

say: It's a big change, but five years is **long enough** for people who work hard.
I'd suggest retraining buyers into **advisers** who visit farms.
think: At thirty-two I'd plan to have a **business with staff**, maybe a few shops.
I'd have used the five years **well**.
do: **Register** my side business and buy a small stake in a farm supply shop.
Keep learning the tools, since they're my edge, and save for a **house deposit**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but pushed forward, which is a good type of pressure.
S3.quote: Five years means I can stack things: business, share, savings, house.
fieldNote: Liam likes five years because he can **stack** things, in the order of business, share, savings, house.
He already has a partner in mind: **Raj**, a farm shop owner he trusts.

steps.text: Register my stock-planning side business within the first year
Buy a small stake in Raj's farm supply shop
Keep using AI forecasting at Greenacre to stay ahead
Save 400 a month for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I'd choose if I could pick the date. At work I'd say let's spend the decade building things. Online I'd say it's good for people who work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm. At thirty-seven I'd expect to have my own business, maybe two shops, and possibly a family. Ten years lets me do all of it without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, grow the business and bring on a second person. I'd buy a house and have the children Hannah and I talk about, perhaps two. And I'd keep using the tools, and look at automating parts of the shop's ordering myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A little guilty, because I know not everyone has the same options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change about the way you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes it a normal career with a big twist. I'd keep working hard but with a goal in front. The danger isn't fear, it's getting comfortable and doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you put your effort first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First the business, since that takes time to grow. Then the house, then the family. I'd also pay back something to my uncle, maybe helping him with a robot milker when the time comes.

say: It's what I'd choose if I could pick the date; let's spend the decade **building things**.
It's good for people who **work for it**.
think: At thirty-seven I'd expect to have my **own business**, maybe two shops, and possibly a family.
Ten years lets me do all of it **without panic**.
do: Grow the business and bring on a **second person** while keeping my job.
Buy a **house**, have children with Hannah and automate the shop's ordering myself.
feel: **Relaxed**, with a little guilt because not everyone has the same options.
S4.quote: The danger isn't fear, it's getting comfortable and doing nothing.
fieldNote: Liam is calm and sees the real danger as **comfort**: drifting and doing nothing.
He plans to **repay** his uncle by helping with machinery on the dairy farm.

steps.text: Grow my stock-planning business and hire a second person
Automate the shop's ordering with my own forecasting model
Buy a house and plan a family with Hannah
Put 10 percent of income into shares every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because there wouldn't be time to build the business, and I'd be relying on three months of savings. What would help is clear dates from Greenacre, less red tape for anyone starting a small business, and training that employers help to pay for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptive isn't a guarantee. I use the tools, I'm ahead of most, and I still know I could be out. I just plan like I will be.

headlineQuote: I use the tools, I'm ahead of most, and I still know I could be out. I just plan like I will be.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of farm supplies who uses AI daily and lives with Hannah, a vet nurse.
He grew up around his uncle's **dairy farm**, which gives him a fallback and a feel for customers.
He is free-market and traditional, blames **red tape**, and wants less interference and more help to start businesses.
His mood runs from **calm** through **anxious** at two years and back to **calm** at ten.
His answer to every case is to **own something**: a side business, a stake or a farm shop partnership.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: no time to build the business, and only three months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear dates** from Greenacre, less red tape for small businesses and employer-funded training.
